scenes.title: Start with a proposed promise
scenes.narration: A value proposition describes whom you help, which task or problem you address and what benefit you propose. It is a working promise, not proof. Start with the customer evidence review and keep unresolved assumptions visible.

scenes.title: Choose one claim
scenes.narration: Understanding asks whether someone can explain the offer in their own words. Relevance asks how it connects to their context. Behaviour asks what they actually do in a permitted task. These are different claims; a compliment cannot establish them all.

scenes.title: Show only what exists
scenes.visual: Fictional concept card with prototype label
scenes.narration: Choose the smallest honest stimulus: a concept card, mock-up or demo. Label missing capabilities and untested benefits. Do not present a prototype as a working service or promise speed, savings or results you have not established.

scenes.title: Use a neutral check
scenes.visual: Interviewer gives a fictional task without coaching
scenes.narration: For understanding, ask what they think the offer does and for whom. For relevance, ask about a recent context and current alternative. For behaviour, define a permitted task and observe without leading. Participation and data handling must be appropriate.

scenes.title: Define evidence before testing
scenes.narration: Decide what you will record and what would support, weaken or leave the claim inconclusive before the test. Separate observed actions from reported preferences. Preserve source and context; do not invent counts or market-wide conclusions.

scenes.title: Build the brief
scenes.narration: Create your Value Proposition Test Brief with one claim, honest stimulus, method, evidence rule and safeguards. This lesson prepares a test; it conducts none. Adoption, retention, payment and feasibility remain separate questions.

sections.label: 02 / LEARN
sections.heading: Test one promise, with evidence that fits.

children: A
value proposition
is a proposed customer benefit. A
test claim
is one part you want to check. A
stimulus
is what you show, such as an honest concept card or mock-up.
Understanding
Can a relevant person explain the offer and audience in their own words? Prompt: “What do you think this does, and for whom?” Clarity does not prove demand.
Relevance
Does the proposed benefit relate to a recent task and current alternative? Ask about that context without suggesting agreement. Reported relevance does not prove adoption.
Behaviour
What does the person actually do in a permitted task? Observe the action and context; keep preference, purchase and repeated use separate.
Evidence limits
“I like it” is a compliment. A demo action is a bounded observation. Neither automatically demonstrates payment, retention or a market-wide result.
Use your evidence review to choose a customer/task and current alternative.
Write a proposed benefit with unproven parts labeled.
Select one claim: understanding, relevance or behaviour.
Show the smallest honest stimulus; disclose missing capabilities.
Define neutral prompts/task and observable evidence before testing.
Set a review rule, alternative explanations and stop conditions.
Illustrative planned check

Concept: one clear registration entry point for first-time visitors. Claim: a relevant adult can explain what the concept does without coaching. Stimulus: labeled concept card, no working registration service. Evidence: their own-word explanation, recorded with appropriate permission. Review rule: unclear/misunderstood meaning weakens clarity; a clear explanation supports clarity only. Access pending; no test conducted.

Never invent a speed or cost-saving number to strengthen the promise. Use anonymous planning notes here; contact details and actual personal source material belong in an approved secure system. This lesson designs a check, sends no messages and collects no payments.
